title: Chemical nomenclature: ions, compounds and acids
note: Ionic compounds name the cation, then the anion; a metal with more than one common charge gets a Roman numeral, as in iron(III). Oxyanions with more oxygen end in -ate, with less in -ite. For acids, -ide becomes hydro-…-ic acid, -ate becomes -ic acid, and -ite becomes -ous acid. Molecular compounds use prefixes: mono, di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa.

read.title: Reading a chemical name
text: Chemical names follow a small set of rules, and once you know them a name tells you the formula. For an ionic compound, name the cation and then the anion. A simple anion ends in -ide, so Na₂O is sodium oxide. Many transition metals form more than one ion, so the charge goes in Roman numerals: FeCl₂ is iron(II) chloride and FeCl₃ is iron(III) chloride. The formula itself is whatever ratio makes the charges cancel.

Polyatomic ions keep their own names. Several are oxyanions, which pair an element with oxygen. The ion with more oxygen atoms ends in -ate and the one with one fewer oxygen ends in -ite, as with nitrate, NO₃⁻, and nitrite, NO₂⁻. Chlorine has four: hypochlorite, chlorite, chlorate, and perchlorate, from fewest oxygens to most.
Compounds of two nonmetals use Greek prefixes instead of charges, because no ions are involved. CO is carbon monoxide and SF₆ is sulfur hexafluoride.

Acids are named from their anions. An -ide anion gives a hydro-…-ic acid, so chloride gives hydrochloric acid. An -ate anion gives an -ic acid, so nitrate gives nitric acid. An -ite anion gives an -ous acid, so nitrite gives nitrous acid.
